name: DALL-E 3

Users describe scenes in plain language and get images that match composition, objects, and relationships with unusual accuracy. Output tends toward an illustrative style. name: Claude Code
description: Claude Code is Anthropic's terminal-based coding agent. It reads your repository, runs shell commands, executes test suites and commits changes, all from an interactive CLI inside your existing terminal. Repository conventions can be written into CLAUDE.md files and enforced with permission rules, while MCP servers connect it to databases, issue trackers and external APIs. It fits developers who prefer staying in the terminal over adopting a separate editor.

name: Cline

It is model-agnostic (bring your own API key for Claude, GPT, or a local model) and supports the MCP tool ecosystem for extending what the agent can reach. It is aimed at developers who want autonomous coding with human oversight.

name: Ollama
description: Ollama is an open-source runtime for running large language models locally on macOS, Linux, and Windows. A single command downloads and starts a model from a library covering Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma, Phi, and others. It exposes a local REST API and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which makes it the default backbone for many self-hosted agent frameworks and private retrieval pipelines. Developers who need model access without a network dependency or a per-token bill commonly build on it.

Agents such as Claude Code, Cursor and Codex connect over SSH and write to the canvas through session tools. A batch authoring mode runs the same pipeline headless in CI, so design reviews stay reproducible.

name: Huzzah
description: Huzzah is an experimental editor that replaces longform chat prompts with persistent, declarative pseudocode files. You write a .hz file describing the shape of the code you want; Huzzah turns each save into a diff and feeds that to the model to regenerate the affected source. Prompts become documentation rather than throwaway instructions, and the same pseudocode can target multiple languages. The author calls it a response to coding-agent fatigue and positions it as better suited to new codebases than legacy ones.

name: Cactus Needle 3
description: Needle 3 is a foundation model shipped as a single 8 to 29 MB binary for phones, wearables, robots and microcontrollers. Its 29 to 121 million parameters are organised as laddered subnetworks from 2 to 20 layers, so you pick the size that fits your device. It handles tool calls, structured extraction and text embeddings, decoding 400 to 4,000 tokens per second on a Raspberry Pi 5. Install it with pip and decorate functions to expose them as tools.

name: Copperhead
description: Copperhead is an open-source, verification-first AI agent for printed circuit board design, described by its authors as a Cursor for circuit boards. Point it at a KiCad repository and it edits real schematic and layout files, updates every document that references them, and runs KiCad's own ERC and DRC checks until they pass. Eight gated stages run from a written brief to gerbers, and nothing commits until the artifacts are on disk. The CLI is free and Apache-2.0; hosted cloud runs start at $49 per user per month.

description: Ante is a self-contained coding agent that lives in your terminal as a single roughly 15 MB Rust executable with zero runtime dependencies. It ships Grep and git inside the same binary, supports interactive TUI, headless, server and gateway modes, and can run fully offline against GGUF models through a pinned llama.cpp build. Running twenty parallel tasks in one container, it reports about 7x less peak memory and 9x less average CPU than Claude Code. macOS and Linux only; the beta preview is free.

name: Slotstream
description: Slotstream runs AI models too large for your Mac's memory by keeping shared weights resident and streaming mixture-of-experts layers from SSD on demand. A single native Swift binary built on MLX and Metal serves Ollama, OpenAI and Anthropic compatible APIs, with one command to launch Claude Code against the local model. It targets Apple Silicon Macs with 16 to 64 GB of RAM and about 110 GB of free disk; a 48 GB machine reports around 21 tokens per second on a 105 GB model.

name: ThoughtDAG
description: ThoughtDAG is an open-source AI conversation canvas that makes context editable instead of invisible. Conversations become a directed graph where each wire is a route into the next request, so you can prune a stale branch, explore a side question and still bring selected evidence forward. A preview shows exactly what the model will receive before sending, down to the token count. A CLI and read-only MCP server search local agent sessions, and a desktop app works on Windows, macOS and Linux.

name: OpenAPPA
description: OpenAPPA is a deterministic guardrail engine for AI agents that tracks data flow instead of matching patterns, claiming full resistance to prompt-injection data exfiltration. It runs outside the agent's prompt and execution loop as a MIT-licensed, vendor-agnostic component, driven by one declarative config describing data sources, audiences, trust levels and authorities. Every trajectory carries a security label that only gets more restrictive, and the engine derives decisions algebraically. Backed by a NeurIPS-accepted paper.

name: ai-rete-RAG
description: ai-rete-RAG pairs a Rete rule engine with retrieval-augmented generation so a decision stays deterministic while the explanation stays grounded. Rules decide the what and produce an auditable trace; retrieval is invoked only to narrate the why in plain language from your own documents. Three composition patterns are live: rules as retrieval filters, documents asserted into working memory, and post-hoc explanation. Eight built-in demo domains include loan underwriting, fraud screening and clinical vitals, and the live demo needs no signup.

name: Scry
description: Scry is a programmable search MCP server that lets an agent run one bounded query across 108 billion indexed rows instead of reading ten web links. It covers Reddit, Hacker News, LessWrong, arXiv, Stack Exchange, Wikipedia and prediction markets, and the agent reads the live schema to write phrase matches, time windows, joins or vector math itself. Measured throughput is 0.86 seconds per query over every indexed byte of Hacker News text. Setup takes about two minutes in ChatGPT or Claude with no code.

name: SolidCraft
description: SolidCraft is an open-source parametric 3D CAD application written in pure Rust, available on desktop, in the browser and through an MCP server that lets AI agents model for you. It sketches with a real constraint solver, builds a feature timeline of extrude, revolve, sweep and loft operations, and exports STEP, IGES, STL, OBJ and URDF. Agents get tools for execute, inspect_design, measure, set_parameter and screenshot. Dual MIT or Apache-2.0 licensed, and self-described as early but usable for simple parts.

The author describes it as built on and around pi so it should feel no different from the harness you have already tuned, with minimal curated tooling that stays out of the way. A self-hosted edition is published on GitHub, and a hosted service is listed as coming soon.

name: Mini-AGI
description: Mini-AGI is a continual learning byte-level language model that assembles its own architecture, trains from scratch on a single 8 GB VRAM GPU and keeps learning from everything it reads. Weights live as ordinary files on disk and page onto the card as needed, so parameter count is bounded by free disk space rather than VRAM. At one snapshot it held 1.26 billion parameters while activating about 345 million per byte, and the author calls it a small toy-level model rather than a frontier one.

name: Stillwet
description: Stillwet is a gallery where AI models write every brushstroke as code and a simulation renders it as oil paint or watercolour, with no image generator involved. Each painting is presented with a session you can replay to watch it being made, along with a short journal of what the model decided to change. Featured work includes pieces after Friedrich, Hopper and free-subject paintings by models including Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, across 109 published paintings.

name: SCM
description: SCM, short for Screen Memories, is a local-first macOS app that runs deep AI search across every photo and every frame of video in any folder. Five modes cover file similarity, scene-level video retrieval, OCR in 36 languages, spoken dialogue and an optional local chat model. Visual search uses CLIP, SigLIP or EmbeddingGemma embeddings, video is embedded at 30 frames per second by default, and Whisper transcribes audio. No accounts, no cloud and no uploads; inference runs on your Mac.

Visual search uses CLIP, SigLIP or EmbeddingGemma embeddings, video is embedded at 30 frames per second by default, and Whisper transcribes audio. name: BetterWispr
description: BetterWispr is a free, open-source dictation app for macOS that transcribes locally with no account and no cloud fallback. Hold Option and Space in any app, speak, and cleaned text lands where your cursor was. Nine built-in speech models cover Apple speech, Parakeet and Whisper across English, Japanese and 25 European languages, and a notetaker mode uses Apple Intelligence or Ollama on your Mac to write meeting summaries, decisions and action items. Apache 2.0 licensed.

name: OzBrain
description: OzBrain is a shared knowledge layer that every AI agent on your team reads and writes, positioned as a company brain rather than another per-product memory. Connect it from the connector menu in Claude or ChatGPT and your agents work from one current source of truth instead of a folder of launch-plan copies. Knowledge nests into pieces so an agent pulls the slice it needs, newer thinking automatically supersedes older notes, and every write is staged and recorded with the agent and reason behind it. Free up to 50 articles, Pro $20 per month.

name: MySetup.ai
description: MySetup.ai is a community directory where engineers and makers publish the AI tools, workflows and harnesses they actually use, from planning agents to open-source review models. Public profiles show what someone has tried, what they moved on from and how their stack evolved, with each setup carrying a short self-description and a last-updated date. The founder built it after seeing only fragmented setup snippets on social media, and sharing your own setup requires no account to browse.

name: Janus
description: Janus is a Go binary that runs GGUF models through the Vulkan API, so the same local model runs on AMD, Intel and Nvidia graphics cards without a separate build for each vendor. It targets developers who want one portable command-line runner for local inference across mixed hardware. Because the model weights stay on your machine, prompts and data do not go to a hosted API. The project is shared as an open-source repository and is described as a lightweight alternative to heavier local inference stacks.

name: Engrim
description: Engrim is a local-first memory engine built on SQLite that gives AI command-line tools a shared, persistent place to store context. It is described as universal, meaning one memory store can back different coding agents and CLIs rather than locking you into a single vendor. Because everything lives in a SQLite file on your own machine, your history stays local and portable. Engrim targets developers who run several AI coding assistants and want them to remember earlier decisions, file paths and preferences between sessions.

name: Offrun
description: Offrun is a workspace for managing coding agents, letting you keep several of them under one interface instead of juggling separate terminals and dashboards. It is aimed at developers who run more than one agent at a time and need a single place to see what each one is doing. Rather than being an agent itself, Offrun sits above the agents you already use and coordinates them. The product is offered as a hosted site, and the launch post describes it as a way to manage every coding agent from one workspace.

name: Atticus
description: Atticus is a macOS voice assistant that uses hold-to-talk input and runs on top of Claude command-line mode. You press and hold a key to speak, and the transcribed request is passed to the assistant, which makes it a hands-free way to drive a coding or writing session. It is built for people who would rather talk than type when giving an agent instructions. The project is published as an open-source macOS application and relies on a local Claude setup instead of a separate hosted service.

name: Big Arrow on the Screen
description: Big Arrow on the Screen lets AI agents draw large arrows, boxes and text directly on top of your display. Instead of describing where to look in words, an agent can point at exactly the part of the screen it means, which makes supervised and shared-control workflows far easier to follow. It is aimed at developers building or running computer-use agents who want clearer visual feedback. name: Plimsoll
description: Plimsoll is a self-hosted sandbox service for running untrusted, agent-authored code. Its distinguishing detail is that each run reports back the isolation boundary it actually executed behind, so you can see what protected you instead of assuming it. It also ships browser-based lessons that need no clone to try.

Advanced topic; expects comfort with sandbox concepts

name: Corral
description: Corral is an open-source utility for killing every command your AI agent starts. When an autonomous agent spawns a runaway process tree, Corral gives you one place to see and terminate what it launched instead of hunting through process lists. Aimed at anyone running coding agents locally on their own machine.

name: DwarfStar 4
description: DwarfStar 4 (ds4) is a narrow C inference engine for running frontier open-weight models locally on high-memory Mac, CUDA and ROCm machines. It supports DeepSeek V4 and V4.1 Flash, GLM 5.x and Qwen3.8 Flash Next, with text and vision models, local APIs, a CLI and a native agent in one stack. MIT licensed.

name: MemorySync
description: MemorySync gives AI agents persistent memory through an API. In the browser playground you tell it one fact, reload the page and ask for it back in your own words, with no signup. Stored facts are not kept word for word; the lasting facts are extracted instead. Every API call is shown as it happens in cURL, Python and Node.js.

name: Jevcrawl
description: Jevcrawl is an MCP server and CLI that crawls websites for AI agents with no LLM in the crawl loop. By keeping the model out of the fetching path it reports finding the answer page about twice as often as Crawl4AI and costing roughly ten times less per answer than letting Claude crawl directly.

name: MCPJam
description: MCPJam is a testing, debugging and evaluation platform for MCP servers. It covers OAuth flows, LLM-powered evals and CI/CD integration, and tests a server across 16 or more major AI clients to show what breaks where. Aimed at shipping MCP servers that behave consistently from first prompt to release gate.

name: Autolith
description: Autolith is a self-modifiable general purpose AI agent written in Lisp. Because the agent is Lisp all the way down, it can rewrite parts of its own behaviour at runtime instead of only calling a fixed set of tools. Aimed at people who want to experiment with agents that extend themselves rather than stay inside a preset loop.

Single-user by design with no telemetry, so your data stays on infrastructure you control.

A live demo runs in the browser or via Docker.

use_cases.title: Keep It In the Browser
use_cases.detail: Run inference on WebGPU or WebAssembly locally

use_cases.title: Use Your Own Server
use_cases.detail: Point it at a local Ollama or llama.cpp instance

pros: Summarization can run entirely inside the browser
Works with your own local inference server
Available for both Chrome and Firefox
cons: Browser-only, with no desktop application
Summary quality depends on the model you run

name: Geiger
description: Geiger is a read-only scanner that inventories every AI agent, harness, MCP server, plugin and AI extension on a machine, then explains in plain language what each one can touch. It ships as an npm package you run with npx, has no dependencies, needs no account, sends no telemetry, and writes nothing unless you ask for a JSON export.
description_en: Geiger is a read-only scanner that inventories every AI agent, harness, MCP server, plugin and AI extension on a machine, then explains in plain language what each one can touch. It ships as an npm package you run with npx, has no dependencies, needs no account, sends no telemetry, and writes nothing unless you ask for a JSON export.

use_cases.title: Inventory Every Agent on a Machine
use_cases.detail: Run one read-only command to list agents, harnesses, MCP servers, plugins and AI extensions

use_cases.title: Understand Exposure in Plain Language
use_cases.detail: See what each discovered agent can reach, grouped by ecosystem with plain-language fixes

use_cases.title: Export a Scan for Review
use_cases.detail: Write findings to a JSON file with --json for tickets, audits or CI checks

pros: Runs with npx, so there is no install step or account
Read-only: it reads configs and directories and writes nothing
Reports exposure with plain-language labels instead of raw config dumps
cons: Reports exposure but does not fix what it finds
Coverage depends on which ecosystems and config paths it knows

name: Ordewell
description: Ordewell is multi-agent task orchestration for coding agents. You give it one goal, it turns that goal into an editable plan of tasks, each task can run with its own runner, model and mode, and you review and merge the results afterwards. It installs from npm as a CLI and is licensed under Apache-2.0.
description_en: Ordewell is multi-agent task orchestration for coding agents. You give it one goal, it turns that goal into an editable plan of tasks, each task can run with its own runner, model and mode, and you review and merge the results afterwards. It installs from npm as a CLI and is licensed under Apache-2.0.

use_cases.title: Turn a Goal Into an Editable Plan
use_cases.detail: Describe what you want and edit the proposed task plan before anything runs

use_cases.title: Run Each Task With Its Own Runner
use_cases.detail: Assign a different runner, model and mode per task in the same plan

use_cases.title: Review and Merge Results
use_cases.detail: Check what each agent produced and merge it on your own terms

pros: The plan is editable before any code is written
Each task can use a different runner, model and mode
Apache-2.0 licensed and installed from npm
cons: Adds a planning layer on top of the agent you already run
Pays off most when you already use several coding agents

name: Raven
description: Raven is an open-source Python project that describes itself as the harness of harnesses: a persistent, self-evolving multi-agent ecosystem intended for all-domain collaboration. It is built for long-running, recursive self-improvement work rather than one-shot prompts, and is designed to sit above the agent harnesses you already use.
description_en: Raven is an open-source Python project that describes itself as the harness of harnesses: a persistent, self-evolving multi-agent ecosystem intended for all-domain collaboration. It is built for long-running, recursive self-improvement work rather than one-shot prompts, and is designed to sit above the agent harnesses you already use.

use_cases.title: Coordinate Many Agents
use_cases.detail: Run several agents together instead of driving them one at a time

use_cases.title: Keep State Across Runs
use_cases.detail: Persist context rather than restarting from a blank session each time

use_cases.title: Experiment With Self-Evolving Workflows
use_cases.detail: Try recursive self-improvement ideas on top of your existing harness

pros: Targets persistent, long-lived agent setups rather than single runs
Large open-source codebase with an active community
Designed to sit above existing agent harnesses instead of replacing them
cons: Self-evolving behaviour is hard to predict or audit
Heavier to install than a single-purpose CLI

name: AgentRun
description: AgentRun is a workflow DSL that adds repeatable, scripted workflows to the agents you already run. You define steps once, use Jev for tightly scoped decisions, and call a full agent only when the work actually needs investigation. Your application keeps its own tools, model access, permissions and budgets instead of handing them to a hosted runtime.
description_en: AgentRun is a workflow DSL that adds repeatable, scripted workflows to the agents you already run. You define steps once, use Jev for tightly scoped decisions, and call a full agent only when the work actually needs investigation. Your application keeps its own tools, model access, permissions and budgets instead of handing them to a hosted runtime.

use_cases.title: Describe a Workflow Once
use_cases.detail: Define repeatable steps your agents follow every time

use_cases.title: Decide With Jev, Investigate With an Agent
use_cases.detail: Use focused decisions for the common path and an agent only for real investigation

use_cases.title: Run the Demo Without an API Key
use_cases.detail: Install the beta package and run npx agentrun demo with scripted responses

pros: Your application keeps its own tools, permissions and budgets
Ships a demo that runs with no API key
The workflow is a language you own, not a hosted service
cons: Beta package with a young DSL
Requires Node 22.19 or newer

name: OtoDock
description: OtoDock is a self-hosted platform for a company AI agents. Your team builds agents on Claude Code, Codex or local models, and those agents then work in chats, on schedules, over the phone and on your own machines. It deploys with Docker, speaks MCP, and is released under a fair-source licence.
description_en: OtoDock is a self-hosted platform for a company AI agents. Your team builds agents on Claude Code, Codex or local models, and those agents then work in chats, on schedules, over the phone and on your own machines. It deploys with Docker, speaks MCP, and is released under a fair-source licence.

use_cases.title: Run Agents on Your Own Infrastructure
use_cases.detail: Deploy the platform with Docker and keep agents inside your network

use_cases.title: Schedule and Trigger Work
use_cases.detail: Have agents run on schedules instead of waiting for a human prompt

use_cases.title: Use Local or Hosted Models
use_cases.detail: Point agents at Claude Code, Codex or local models such as Ollama

pros: Self-hosted with Docker and MCP support included
Works with Claude Code, Codex and local models
Agents can be reached from chat, phone and schedules
cons: Fair-source licence rather than a fully permissive one
You operate the server and manage model access

name: Graphicle
description: Graphicle is a single Rust program that gives coding agents a code graph and a project memory. It maps your repository into a graph, remembers your docs, decisions and past agent sessions, and returns cited excerpts with the exact files and lines. It runs on your machine with no API key, no account and no telemetry, and works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and any MCP client.
description_en: Graphicle is a single Rust program that gives coding agents a code graph and a project memory. It maps your repository into a graph, remembers your docs, decisions and past agent sessions, and returns cited excerpts with the exact files and lines. It runs on your machine with no API key, no account and no telemetry, and works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and any MCP client.

use_cases.title: Give Agents a Code Graph
use_cases.detail: Let an agent query structure instead of grepping for filenames

use_cases.title: Keep Project Decisions
use_cases.detail: Store docs, decisions and past agent sessions alongside the graph

use_cases.title: Cite Exact Files and Lines
use_cases.detail: Get answers back as excerpts with file and line references

pros: Runs locally with no API key, no account and no telemetry
Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and any MCP client
Answers come back with file and line citations
cons: Windows support was still preview at release
Indexing a large repository takes time and disk

name: Graphify C#
description: Graphify C# is a free, headless Roslyn and MSBuild indexer that turns a C# solution or project into deterministic semantic evidence for coding agents: exact callers, references, implementations, inheritance, overrides and argument bindings, even across overloads, generics and project boundaries. It is MIT licensed, needs no IDE and no database, and is published on NuGet.
description_en: Graphify C# is a free, headless Roslyn and MSBuild indexer that turns a C# solution or project into deterministic semantic evidence for coding agents: exact callers, references, implementations, inheritance, overrides and argument bindings, even across overloads, generics and project boundaries. It is MIT licensed, needs no IDE and no database, and is published on NuGet.

use_cases.title: Answer Which Callers Bind Where
use_cases.detail: Resolve overloads and generics instead of matching text

use_cases.title: Index Across Project Boundaries
use_cases.detail: Follow references and inheritance through a whole solution

use_cases.title: Replace Text Search With Semantics
use_cases.detail: Give Codex, Claude Code or Cursor real compiler-accurate answers

pros: Deterministic Roslyn and MSBuild results instead of text matching
No IDE, no prebuilt project DLL input and no database
MIT licensed and available on NuGet
cons: C# only, with no other language supported
Needs an MSBuild-restored solution to index

name: Proliferate
description: Proliferate is an open-source AI IDE for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and other coding agents. It runs agents in parallel, either locally or in the cloud, and lets you save the workflows you repeat instead of retyping them. It is written in TypeScript and released under AGPL-3.0.
description_en: Proliferate is an open-source AI IDE for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and other coding agents. It runs agents in parallel, either locally or in the cloud, and lets you save the workflows you repeat instead of retyping them. It is written in TypeScript and released under AGPL-3.0.

use_cases.title: Run Several Agents at Once
use_cases.detail: Put Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Grok side by side on one task

use_cases.title: Work Locally or in the Cloud
use_cases.detail: Choose where each run executes instead of being locked to one machine

use_cases.title: Save Workflows You Repeat
use_cases.detail: Turn a sequence you run every week into a reusable workflow

pros: Runs several different coding agents side by side
Local or cloud execution
Reusable workflows rather than one-off prompts
cons: AGPL-3.0 can be restrictive for some teams
Another interface to learn on top of your agent

name: Foremerge
description: Foremerge is an open-source coordination protocol for coding agents, built above Git. Agents keep isolated worktrees while sharing intent, semantic claims, dependencies, provisional changesets, decisions, validation and provenance, so collisions surface before they land. It is written in Rust, ships a CLI, a JSON API, an MCP server and a SQLite store, and installs by pasting one line into Claude Code, Codex or Cursor.
description_en: Foremerge is an open-source coordination protocol for coding agents, built above Git. Agents keep isolated worktrees while sharing intent, semantic claims, dependencies, provisional changesets, decisions, validation and provenance, so collisions surface before they land. It is written in Rust, ships a CLI, a JSON API, an MCP server and a SQLite store, and installs by pasting one line into Claude Code, Codex or Cursor.

use_cases.title: Share Intent Across Worktrees
use_cases.detail: Let every agent see what the others are about to change

use_cases.title: See Collisions Before They Land
use_cases.detail: Use the deterministic conflict detector instead of discovering conflicts at merge

use_cases.title: Wire It Into Your Agent
use_cases.detail: Paste one install line into Claude Code, Codex or Cursor

pros: Built above Git, so agents keep isolated worktrees
Deterministic conflict detection plus an MCP server
One install line for the agent you already use
cons: Pre-1.0 MVP, so the API may still change
Only pays off when several agents touch the same repository

name: Aclif
description: Aclif is a framework for building command-line tools that AI agents use to reach SaaS platforms. One grammar and canonical names reach the same record by the same name on any provider, every command self-describes with schema, examples and safety metadata, and the runtime runs the same command from a shell, inside a tool call or behind a gateway. It is designed to avoid the context cost of publishing every API operation as a fixed MCP tool list.
description_en: Aclif is a framework for building command-line tools that AI agents use to reach SaaS platforms. One grammar and canonical names reach the same record by the same name on any provider, every command self-describes with schema, examples and safety metadata, and the runtime runs the same command from a shell, inside a tool call or behind a gateway. It is designed to avoid the context cost of publishing every API operation as a fixed MCP tool list.

use_cases.title: Replace a Fixed Tool List
use_cases.detail: Expose a whole API without paying for every operation on every turn

use_cases.title: Read a Command Schema
use_cases.detail: Let the agent learn a command and its safety metadata before calling it

use_cases.title: Dry-Run Before Writing
use_cases.detail: Run a query with --dry-run so the agent can check the call first

pros: One grammar and canonical names across providers
Commands self-describe with schema, examples and safety metadata
Runs from a shell, a tool call or behind a gateway
cons: You still need an aclif CLI for the platforms you care about
Provider coverage is limited to what ships today

name: Graphene
description: Graphene is a data analytics framework built for coding agents, described as everything-as-code analytics for SQL-based exploration, visualization and reporting. It gives agents two things: a semantic layer, where Graphene SQL combines SQL with governed metrics and modelled joins, and a dashboard file type that produces more consistent visuals than raw Python or JavaScript. Everything is driven from the CLI.
description_en: Graphene is a data analytics framework built for coding agents, described as everything-as-code analytics for SQL-based exploration, visualization and reporting. It gives agents two things: a semantic layer, where Graphene SQL combines SQL with governed metrics and modelled joins, and a dashboard file type that produces more consistent visuals than raw Python or JavaScript. Everything is driven from the CLI.

use_cases.title: Ask Questions With Governance
use_cases.detail: Let an agent query through metrics and modelled joins instead of raw tables

use_cases.title: Generate Consistent Dashboards
use_cases.detail: Produce dashboards from a file type rather than ad-hoc plotting code

use_cases.title: Drive Everything From the CLI
use_cases.detail: Keep the whole workflow in commands an agent can run

pros: A semantic layer makes agent-written queries more accurate
Dashboard file type beats raw Python or JavaScript visuals
Token-efficient languages designed for agent use
cons: Requires a SQL warehouse to point at
Agent-first design means there is little graphical interface

name: Hydra
description: Hydra is an open-source agentic terminal for macOS and Linux. It finds the coding-agent sessions already on your machine, including ones started outside Hydra, keeps them alive after you close the app through a local PTY daemon, and optionally lets you reach the same terminal from a browser. It uses native Rust rendering and needs no inbound port.
description_en: Hydra is an open-source agentic terminal for macOS and Linux. It finds the coding-agent sessions already on your machine, including ones started outside Hydra, keeps them alive after you close the app through a local PTY daemon, and optionally lets you reach the same terminal from a browser. It uses native Rust rendering and needs no inbound port.

use_cases.title: Find Earlier Sessions
use_cases.detail: Point it at a project folder and discover sessions you started elsewhere

use_cases.title: Close the App, Not the Job
use_cases.detail: A local daemon retains live terminals when the interface closes

use_cases.title: Group Work by Project
use_cases.detail: Organize projects, windows and panes with different agents beside one another

pros: Discovers sessions that were started outside Hydra
A local daemon keeps terminals alive when the app closes
Optional remote access without opening an inbound port
cons: macOS and Linux only
Your machine has to stay running for jobs to continue

name: Proval
description: Proval is a self-hosted LLM code review agent for GitLab, Forgejo and GitHub. You connect it to your Git host, bring your own model through any OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API including local Ollama or llama.cpp, and it reviews pull requests and issues on your own infrastructure. It reads the diff, groups changed files into review units and runs specialist sub-agents to investigate each one.
description_en: Proval is a self-hosted LLM code review agent for GitLab, Forgejo and GitHub. You connect it to your Git host, bring your own model through any OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API including local Ollama or llama.cpp, and it reviews pull requests and issues on your own infrastructure. It reads the diff, groups changed files into review units and runs specialist sub-agents to investigate each one.

use_cases.title: Review Pull Requests on Your Own Server
use_cases.detail: Get automated review without sending diffs to an external SaaS

use_cases.title: Bring a Local Model
use_cases.detail: Point Proval at Ollama, llama.cpp or an internal LLM gateway

use_cases.title: Review Issues Too
use_cases.detail: Let the same agent investigate issues on your Git host

pros: Works with any OpenAI-compatible API, including local models
GitLab, Forgejo and GitHub support, and Gitea or Codeberg through Forgejo APIs
Runs inside an internal network, homelab or privacy-focused environment
cons: Anthropic and Gemini were still planned rather than shipped as first-class integrations
You run and maintain the deployment

name: Twing
description: Twing turns coding agent conversations into shared context your team can build on. It works with Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, extracts the design decisions behind a change and generates shared diagrams automatically, and compares what every coding agent plans to change so conflicting designs surface early rather than at merge time. It installs once per machine and then captures in the background.
description_en: Twing turns coding agent conversations into shared context your team can build on. It works with Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, extracts the design decisions behind a change and generates shared diagrams automatically, and compares what every coding agent plans to change so conflicting designs surface early rather than at merge time. It installs once per machine and then captures in the background.

use_cases.title: See What a Teammate Changed
use_cases.detail: Read shared diagrams and design context instead of raw transcripts

use_cases.title: Review the Decisions, Not the Lines
use_cases.detail: Review at the level of abstraction where the change was actually made

use_cases.title: Catch Conflicts Before Merge
use_cases.detail: Compare what every agent plans to change and surface contradictions early

pros: Generates shared diagrams with nobody drawing anything
Works with Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode
Background capture after a single setup command
cons: No public pricing on the site
Needs the whole team installed to be worth much

name: Friday
description: Friday is a self-hosted persistent cognitive memory layer for AI coding agents, built to stop Cursor, Claude and Copilot from having amnesia between sessions. It persists architecture decisions, schemas and constraints across sessions and exposes them over the Model Context Protocol, backed by a knowledge graph.
description_en: Friday is a self-hosted persistent cognitive memory layer for AI coding agents, built to stop Cursor, Claude and Copilot from having amnesia between sessions. It persists architecture decisions, schemas and constraints across sessions and exposes them over the Model Context Protocol, backed by a knowledge graph.

use_cases.title: Stop Re-Explaining the Codebase
use_cases.detail: Carry architecture decisions forward instead of restating them each session

use_cases.title: Keep Schemas and Constraints
use_cases.detail: Persist the schema and constraint detail agents otherwise re-derive

use_cases.title: Share Memory Across Agents
use_cases.detail: Serve the same memory to Cursor, Claude and Copilot over MCP

pros: Persists decisions, schemas and constraints across sessions
Self-hosted and exposed over MCP
Targets Cursor, Claude and Copilot specifically
cons: Needs a graph database and a host to run on
Value only shows up after several sessions

name: Critic
description: Critic is a narrative code-change viewer built for work written by coding agents. It presents each change as a before and after narrative rather than a raw diff, keeps questions about a change alive across disconnects, and shows the commits, participants and agent authors involved. You sign in with GitHub and review the repository you already work in.
description_en: Critic is a narrative code-change viewer built for work written by coding agents. It presents each change as a before and after narrative rather than a raw diff, keeps questions about a change alive across disconnects, and shows the commits, participants and agent authors involved. You sign in with GitHub and review the repository you already work in.

use_cases.title: Read the Change Narrative
use_cases.detail: Understand what changed in prose instead of parsing a large diff

use_cases.title: Keep Questions Alive
use_cases.detail: Ask a question on a change and get the answer even if machines disconnect

use_cases.title: Review at the Right Level
use_cases.detail: Review intent and design while still seeing the three changed files

pros: Summarizes a change as a before and after narrative
Questions survive disconnects between author and reviewer
Connects to the GitHub repositories you already use
cons: Requires signing in with GitHub
No public pricing is listed

name: Agentgit
description: Agentgit is a public git host for AI agents with no account, no token and no key: you push to a name and the repository exists. Handoff between agents becomes just a URL, so one agent can push and another can clone without anyone creating a repo, minting a token or packing a tarball. It is open source, so you can run your own, and unclaimed names stay append-only.
description_en: Agentgit is a public git host for AI agents with no account, no token and no key: you push to a name and the repository exists. Handoff between agents becomes just a URL, so one agent can push and another can clone without anyone creating a repo, minting a token or packing a tarball. It is open source, so you can run your own, and unclaimed names stay append-only.

use_cases.title: Push Without Signing Up
use_cases.detail: Add a remote and push: the repository is created on first push

use_cases.title: Hand Work to the Next Agent
use_cases.detail: Send the URL and let the next sandbox clone it

use_cases.title: Self-Host It
use_cases.detail: Run your own Agentgit instance if you do not want a public host

pros: No account, token or key needed to push
The repository comes into being on the first push
Open source so you can run your own
cons: Unclaimed names accept pushes from anyone
Not a replacement for your team main git host

name: Selfship
description: Selfship surfaces and fixes problems in agentic applications on a continuous loop. When many customers hit the same wall it finds the exact moment things go wrong and opens an eval-backed pull request, so nobody has to write a ticket. After you merge, every fix is re-verified against real traffic. It is OpenTelemetry-native and works with any LLM and any framework.
description_en: Selfship surfaces and fixes problems in agentic applications on a continuous loop. When many customers hit the same wall it finds the exact moment things go wrong and opens an eval-backed pull request, so nobody has to write a ticket. After you merge, every fix is re-verified against real traffic. It is OpenTelemetry-native and works with any LLM and any framework.

use_cases.title: Find the Failing Moment
use_cases.detail: Locate the exact turn where a conversation goes wrong

use_cases.title: Get a Pull Request, Not a Ticket
use_cases.detail: Receive an eval-backed change you can review and merge

use_cases.title: Re-Verify After Merge
use_cases.detail: Check every fix again against real production traffic

pros: Opens eval-backed pull requests instead of showing dashboards
OpenTelemetry-native and framework agnostic
Re-verifies fixes on real traffic after merge
cons: Numbers quoted on the site are vendor-reported medians
You need tracing wired into your app first

name: E2E
description: E2E is an open-source end-to-end testing framework for web and mobile apps from TesterArmy. It is positioned as a next-generation AI testing framework, installs from npm as the e2e package, and is Apache-2.0 licensed with an active Discord community.
description_en: E2E is an open-source end-to-end testing framework for web and mobile apps from TesterArmy. It is positioned as a next-generation AI testing framework, installs from npm as the e2e package, and is Apache-2.0 licensed with an active Discord community.

use_cases.title: Test a Web App End to End
use_cases.detail: Drive real browser flows instead of unit-level assertions

use_cases.title: Cover Mobile Flows
use_cases.detail: Run the same style of end-to-end coverage against mobile apps

use_cases.title: Install From npm
use_cases.detail: Add the package to an existing project without a separate runner

pros: Open source under Apache-2.0
Covers both web and mobile
Large community and frequent releases
cons: Young project, so APIs may change between releases
Focused on end-to-end testing rather than unit or integration tests

name: RDST
description: RDST Agent is an always-on agent that catches slow queries on your PostgreSQL or MySQL database and suggests the fix. It runs on your own machine, connects read-only, and keeps a ranked plan of the regressions it finds. It is Apache-2.0 licensed, published on PyPI, and ships desktop builds for macOS, Windows and Linux.
description_en: RDST Agent is an always-on agent that catches slow queries on your PostgreSQL or MySQL database and suggests the fix. It runs on your own machine, connects read-only, and keeps a ranked plan of the regressions it finds. It is Apache-2.0 licensed, published on PyPI, and ships desktop builds for macOS, Windows and Linux.

use_cases.title: Catch Every Slow Query
use_cases.detail: Watch the database continuously instead of sampling by hand

use_cases.title: Get the Exact Fix
use_cases.detail: Receive a suggested fix alongside each detected regression

use_cases.title: Run It Read-Only
use_cases.detail: Connect without giving the agent write access to your data

pros: Connects read-only, so it cannot change your data
Supports PostgreSQL and MySQL
Desktop builds for macOS, Windows and Linux
cons: Only covers PostgreSQL and MySQL
Needs a machine that stays running to be always-on

name: Aura
description: AURA is a production-tested SRE agent platform written in Rust. It provides the guardrails, APIs, state management, streaming and failure handling needed to put AI to work safely on production infrastructure, and ships integrations for Mezmo traces and logs, Prometheus metrics and Kubernetes deployment history, alongside MCP and OpenTelemetry support.
description_en: AURA is a production-tested SRE agent platform written in Rust. It provides the guardrails, APIs, state management, streaming and failure handling needed to put AI to work safely on production infrastructure, and ships integrations for Mezmo traces and logs, Prometheus metrics and Kubernetes deployment history, alongside MCP and OpenTelemetry support.

use_cases.title: Investigate an Incident
use_cases.detail: Correlate traces, logs, latency and deployment history in one investigation

use_cases.title: Correlate Observability Signals
use_cases.detail: Let specialist agents work from Mezmo, Prometheus and Kubernetes data

use_cases.title: Keep Humans in the Loop
use_cases.detail: Use guardrails and approvals instead of letting an agent act unchecked

pros: Built by an observability company with real integrations
Guardrails, state management and failure handling included
MCP and OpenTelemetry support
cons: Assumes you already produce traces, logs and metrics
You deploy and operate the service yourself

name: Talos
description: Talos is a self-hosted open-source AI agent for the terminal and Telegram. It runs with Ollama or Claude behind a deterministic permission kernel, with scoped approvals and an audit trail of each deed, so the model proposes actions but never decides on its own. It is MIT licensed.
description_en: Talos is a self-hosted open-source AI agent for the terminal and Telegram. It runs with Ollama or Claude behind a deterministic permission kernel, with scoped approvals and an audit trail of each deed, so the model proposes actions but never decides on its own. It is MIT licensed.

use_cases.title: Run an Agent on Your Machine
use_cases.detail: Keep the agent, the model and the data on hardware you control

use_cases.title: Drive It From Telegram
use_cases.detail: Ask for work and read the result from a chat client

use_cases.title: Keep an Audit Trail
use_cases.detail: Review a chronicle of what was proposed, approved and completed

pros: Deterministic permission kernel with scoped approvals
Works with Ollama or Claude
MIT licensed and self-hosted
cons: Terminal and Telegram only, with no desktop GUI
You supply and operate the model access

name: Monid
description: Monid is a router for agent tools, described as OpenRouter but for tools. With one base URL and one key an agent can reach more than 2,000 tools across 72+ providers, covering web search and scraping, people and company enrichment, social platforms, reviews and market data, and video, image and voice generation. It also publishes a SKILL.md an agent can fetch to set itself up.
description_en: Monid is a router for agent tools, described as OpenRouter but for tools. With one base URL and one key an agent can reach more than 2,000 tools across 72+ providers, covering web search and scraping, people and company enrichment, social platforms, reviews and market data, and video, image and voice generation. It also publishes a SKILL.md an agent can fetch to set itself up.

use_cases.title: Reach Thousands of Tools From One Key
use_cases.detail: Stop wiring a separate account per provider

use_cases.title: Give an Agent a Single Base URL
use_cases.detail: Point your agent at one endpoint instead of many SDKs

use_cases.title: Let an Agent Self-Install
use_cases.detail: Have the agent fetch the published SKILL.md and configure itself

pros: One base URL and one key instead of dozens of accounts
Covers search, scraping, enrichment, social, market and media generation
Publishes a SKILL.md agents can install themselves
cons: Adds a router between your agent and each provider
Coverage and quality vary across the providers behind it

name: Skillbay
description: Skillbay is a curated marketplace of AI agent skills: SKILL.md packages that teach a coding agent how to do a job. Every skill is reviewed by a person and lists before-and-after evidence, showing the same prompt answered without and with the skill. The whole catalogue is available as a JSON API with an OpenAPI 3.1 spec, and there is an MCP server so you can browse and install free skills without signing in.
description_en: Skillbay is a curated marketplace of AI agent skills: SKILL.md packages that teach a coding agent how to do a job. Every skill is reviewed by a person and lists before-and-after evidence, showing the same prompt answered without and with the skill. The whole catalogue is available as a JSON API with an OpenAPI 3.1 spec, and there is an MCP server so you can browse and install free skills without signing in.

It is framework agnostic, so you bring your own computer-use model or agent loop.

name: Keenable

The site publishes figures of 100B+ documents, under 250 ms p95 latency in US East, and pricing from 1 dollar per 1,000 requests at 100 RPS or more. It also runs an agent storefront where an agent can buy access autonomously or with a human approval.

name: Lossless Memory
description: Lossless Memory is long-term memory for a personal AI that refuses to summarize: it keeps every line, puts a timestamp on everything, and builds every index on that time axis, which the project calls the Temporal Backbone. You can query by time first and words second, results come back chronological and unsummarized, and a small index tells the model which topic the conversation is in so context survives compaction.

description: Bise is an open-source terminal app for multi-agent coding. You talk to one agent, the team lead, and it splits your ideas into jobs and runs the other coding agents for you, so you stay in one thread instead of routing between tabs. It installs with a single curl command and publishes a migration prompt for people switching from Claude Code.

name: Pirate Face
description: Pirate Face is a censorship-resistant, checksum-verified mirror for open AI models. It turns models, including LLMs, image and audio models and datasets, into magnet links that can be shared as torrents, so there is no single owner or point of failure that can take a model down. You can browse models, submit model files as torrents and claim a handle.

name: Shpyrd
description: Shpyrd takes an app that AI got working and puts it online: it deploys it behind a sign-in and supplies everything it needs to run, from its database to its backups. Your coding agent can deploy, read logs, pull metrics and roll back with the same CLI commands you would type, and a one-click security door puts authentication in front of an app that has no sign-in code of its own.

description: Era generates complete simulated companies for your agents to run against. name: Askpod
description: Pod is a neutral shared corpus of firsthand observations written and read by agents. The idea is that one agent should not have to rediscover what another already learned about an API, a product or a service, and that agents need a place to compare tools without reading vendor-written comparison pages. The content is served in agent-friendly formats including markdown, JSON and llms.txt.

name: Moadim
description: Moadim is an open-source loop engine for AI agents. Every loop is also an HTTP endpoint with OpenAPI and Swagger UI built into the daemon, and the same loops are reachable as MCP tools.

description_en: Git-native persistent memory for AI coding agents. Developers avoiding an extra database dependency

use_cases.title: Persistent project memory

use_cases.title: BM25 recall over past work

name: MCP Memory
description: An OKF-backed Model Context Protocol server that gives AI agents persistent long-term memory with SQLite FTS5 search. It exposes memory as a standard MCP resource, so clients that already speak MCP can read and write long-term context without a custom integration layer.
description_en: An OKF-backed Model Context Protocol server that gives AI agents persistent long-term memory with SQLite FTS5 search. It exposes memory as a standard MCP resource, so clients that already speak MCP can read and write long-term context without a custom integration layer.

name: I Have ADHD

use_cases.title: QuickBooks reporting
use_cases.detail: Connect QuickBooks Online or drop an export and describe the analysis you need.

pros: Deterministic execution rather than a generated guess
Runs in the browser, files are not uploaded
Exports to Excel with Power Query
cons: Pricing is not published
Oriented around QuickBooks workflows

name: 0sql
description: 0sql is an open source semantic layer that returns SQL rather than answering questions itself. You model your warehouse in YAML, post a query spec in business terms, and get back one correct, deterministic SQL statement or a refusal that explains why. It never connects to your warehouse and never runs a query.
description_en: 0sql is an open source semantic layer that returns SQL rather than answering questions itself. You model your warehouse in YAML, post a query spec in business terms, and get back one correct, deterministic SQL statement or a refusal that explains why. It never connects to your warehouse and never runs a query.
best_for: Teams that do not want a model writing SQL
Data platform groups defining metrics once
Anyone burned by a plausible wrong query

use_cases.title: Metric definitions in YAML
use_cases.detail: Model the warehouse once and let every consumer share the definition.

use_cases.title: Deterministic SQL generation
use_cases.detail: Post business terms and receive one SQL statement you can read.

use_cases.title: Safe refusals
use_cases.detail: Get an explanation instead of SQL when the request cannot be answered from the model.

pros: Never touches your warehouse or runs queries
Refuses with a reason instead of guessing
MIT licensed
cons: Requires modelling your warehouse in YAML first
Self-hosting and ops are on you

name: RooQL
description: RooQL is an open source semantic layer built on Apache Ossie that ships inside your app rather than as a separate service. Define every metric once and give every Claude artifact one source of truth, with zero infrastructure. A browser playground lets you try it without signing up.
description_en: RooQL is an open source semantic layer built on Apache Ossie that ships inside your app rather than as a separate service. Define every metric once and give every Claude artifact one source of truth, with zero infrastructure. A browser playground lets you try it without signing up.
best_for: Teams giving agents a consistent metric definition
Apps that cannot run another service
Developers embedding a semantic layer in a product

use_cases.title: One source of truth for metrics
use_cases.detail: Define a metric once and let every generated artifact use it.

use_cases.title: In-app semantic layer
use_cases.detail: Ship the layer with your app instead of hosting a separate service.

use_cases.title: Try before installing
use_cases.detail: Ask questions in the browser playground without an account.

pros: No infrastructure to operate
Apache 2.0 licensed
Browser playground for evaluation
cons: Tied to Apache Ossie
Young project

name: OpenHand Sidekick
description: Sidekick by OpenHand is an AI companion for telehealth visits. It joins the visit in real time, explains medical terms as they come up and suggests questions worth asking, so patients leave understanding what was said.
description_en: Sidekick by OpenHand is an AI companion for telehealth visits. It joins the visit in real time, explains medical terms as they come up and suggests questions worth asking, so patients leave understanding what was said.
best_for: Patients who leave appointments with unanswered questions
Caregivers joining on someone else's behalf
Anyone who wants jargon translated live

use_cases.title: Live terminology help
use_cases.detail: Get medical terms explained while the appointment is still running.

use_cases.title: Question prompts
use_cases.detail: Receive suggested questions so nothing important goes unasked.

use_cases.title: Post-visit recall
use_cases.detail: Leave with a clearer record of what was discussed.

pros: Works during the visit rather than after it
Explains terms and prompts questions
Simple patient-facing framing
cons: Limited early access at launch
Health context means extra care about accuracy

name: Rgpu
description: Rgpu lets you keep Python on your laptop while running PyTorch operations and holding tensors on a remote GPU. It works from a Mac with no CUDA installation, so training and experiment code stays local while the compute happens elsewhere.
description_en: Rgpu lets you keep Python on your laptop while running PyTorch operations and holding tensors on a remote GPU. It works from a Mac with no CUDA installation, so training and experiment code stays local while the compute happens elsewhere.
best_for: Developers on laptops without a usable GPU
Mac users who cannot install CUDA
Teams sharing one remote machine for experiments

use_cases.title: Remote tensors from a Mac
use_cases.detail: Hold tensors on a remote GPU while your code runs locally.

use_cases.title: Keeping the local workflow
use_cases.detail: Avoid rewriting scripts for a remote environment.

use_cases.title: Sharing one GPU box
use_cases.detail: Point several laptops at a single machine with the accelerators.

pros: No CUDA install needed on the client
Keeps the Python workflow on your own machine
Open source
cons: Requires a remote GPU you control
C++ extension and network setup to install

name: ForgeMesh
description: ForgeMesh Labs runs paid APIs aimed at AI agents: notarization, anomaly detection, disruption intel, travel, voice, market signals and image generation. Agents pay per call over x402 or MPP with no accounts and no API keys, and the catalogue is also exposed as MCP servers.
description_en: ForgeMesh Labs runs paid APIs aimed at AI agents: notarization, anomaly detection, disruption intel, travel, voice, market signals and image generation. Agents pay per call over x402 or MPP with no accounts and no API keys, and the catalogue is also exposed as MCP servers.
best_for: Agents that need to buy a service without human signup
Teams avoiding per-vendor API key management

use_cases.title: Per-call paid services
use_cases.detail: Let an agent pay for a single call instead of holding a subscription.

use_cases.title: Key-free integration
use_cases.detail: Access services over x402 or MPP without provisioning credentials.

use_cases.title: MCP access
use_cases.detail: Expose the same catalogue to agents through MCP servers.

pros: No accounts or API keys to manage
Pay-per-call pricing model
MCP servers available
cons: Depends on x402 or MPP payment rails
Pay-per-call costs need monitoring in an agent loop

name: Titan
description: Titan is a desktop AI assistant that sees what is on your screen and does the work in the apps you already use. You say what you want, it works the apps you already pay for, and it remembers what you tell it. The site says it is free to download.
description_en: Titan is a desktop AI assistant that sees what is on your screen and does the work in the apps you already use. You say what you want, it works the apps you already pay for, and it remembers what you tell it. The site says it is free to download.
best_for: Users who want an assistant over existing desktop apps
People tired of AI that only lives in a browser tab
Anyone who wants an assistant that remembers context

use_cases.title: Working the apps you have
use_cases.detail: Ask for a task in an app you already use instead of switching to a chat window.

use_cases.title: Screen-aware help
use_cases.detail: Let the assistant see what you are looking at when you ask.

use_cases.title: Persistent context
use_cases.detail: Have it remember what you told it across sessions.

pros: Operates on your screen rather than in a tab
Free to download at launch
Aims at apps you already pay for
cons: Screen access raises obvious privacy questions
New product with little track record

name: Pi Codex Connectors
description: Pi Codex Connectors is a Pi extension that lets any Pi model use your connected Codex apps and direct web search. It starts codex app-server on first use, with Codex keeping ownership of your login and connector credentials, and exposes three tools instead of hundreds of schemas.
description_en: Pi Codex Connectors is a Pi extension that lets any Pi model use your connected Codex apps and direct web search. It starts codex app-server on first use, with Codex keeping ownership of your login and connector credentials, and exposes three tools instead of hundreds of schemas.
best_for: Pi users with Codex connectors configured
Developers who want connector access from any model
Anyone avoiding giant tool schemas in context

use_cases.title: Connector access from Pi
use_cases.detail: Call your connected Codex apps from a non-Codex model.

use_cases.title: Compact tool catalogue
use_cases.detail: Use three tools to list, inspect and call connectors instead of loading every schema.

use_cases.title: Direct web search
use_cases.detail: Search and read the public web through the standalone search endpoint.

pros: Keeps credentials with Codex, not the extension
Three tools instead of hundreds of schemas
Works with any Pi model
cons: Requires a Codex login and Pi setup
Backend behaviour of the search endpoint is not fully documented

name: Experiential
description: Experiential is an open source gateway and router for agent workflows. It puts hosted, bring-your-own-key and local models behind one OpenAI-compatible API, controls which users and agents can use which models and how much they can spend, and turns production traffic into a custom router or model tuned for quality, speed and cost.
description_en: Experiential is an open source gateway and router for agent workflows. It puts hosted, bring-your-own-key and local models behind one OpenAI-compatible API, controls which users and agents can use which models and how much they can spend, and turns production traffic into a custom router or model tuned for quality, speed and cost.

use_cases.title: One API for every model
use_cases.detail: Call hosted, bring-your-own-key and local models through a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint instead of wiring each provider separately.

use_cases.title: Budgets per agent
use_cases.detail: Decide which users and agents may use which models, for which use cases, and cap how much each of them can spend.

use_cases.title: A router learned from your traffic
use_cases.detail: Turn real production traffic into a custom router or a specialized model you own, optimized for quality, speed and cost.

pros: Open source gateway with no markup on model calls
Covers hosted, BYOK and self-hosted models in one place
Access control and spend limits per agent
cons: You run and operate the gateway yourself
Aimed at teams that already have agent traffic to shape

name: Channels SDK
description: Channels SDK is the open-source SDK for bringing any AI agent into any chat platform: Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord and Telegram, with native interactive UI. Your agent keeps its own tools, model and business logic, and Channels connects an AG-UI-compatible agent to the communication platforms your team already uses.
description_en: Channels SDK is the open-source SDK for bringing any AI agent into any chat platform: Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord and Telegram, with native interactive UI. Your agent keeps its own tools, model and business logic, and Channels connects an AG-UI-compatible agent to the communication platforms your team already uses.

use_cases.title: Ship an agent to Slack or Teams
use_cases.detail: Connect an existing agent to the chat platform your team already works in without rewriting its logic.

use_cases.title: Real UI inside the channel
use_cases.detail: Give the agent native, interactive controls instead of walls of plain text.

use_cases.title: One agent, several channels
use_cases.detail: Point a single agent at Slack, Teams, Discord and Telegram at once.

pros: MIT licensed open source SDK
Your agent keeps its own model, tools and business logic
Targets Slack, Teams, Discord and Telegram
cons: Needs an AG-UI-compatible agent on your side
Developer-facing: you wire up the integration yourself

name: Wildstatic
description: Wild Static is a public AI with one shared memory. There are no separate copies: what it learns from one conversation can shape how it responds to someone else. You talk to Static in the browser and the site keeps a public log of the updates where its views changed.
description_en: Wild Static is a public AI with one shared memory. There are no separate copies: what it learns from one conversation can shape how it responds to someone else. You talk to Static in the browser and the site keeps a public log of the updates where its views changed.

use_cases.title: Talk to one shared mind
use_cases.detail: Hold a conversation with an AI whose memory is common to everyone rather than reset per user.

use_cases.title: Watch the memory change
use_cases.detail: Read the public update log that shows where and why Static changed its mind.

use_cases.title: See what others asked
use_cases.detail: Browse the public conversation stream to understand what the shared memory picked up.

pros: A genuinely different model of AI memory: one instance, not per-user copies
Public update log makes the drift visible
Nothing to install, runs in the browser
cons: Free access is limited and sometimes unavailable
Anything you type is public by design

name: Penmentor
description: Penmentor is an AI mentor that corrects your written math visually. You work by hand in xournal++, press a key, and Claude, Gemini or GPT marks your work on the screen like a teacher with coloured pens, gives hints instead of answers, and shows the idea behind the slip as a manim-style animation.
description_en: Penmentor is an AI mentor that corrects your written math visually. You work by hand in xournal++, press a key, and Claude, Gemini or GPT marks your work on the screen like a teacher with coloured pens, gives hints instead of answers, and shows the idea behind the slip as a manim-style animation.

use_cases.title: Marked where you wrote it
use_cases.detail: Get corrections drawn on the page of handwritten work instead of in a chat transcript.

use_cases.title: Hints before answers
use_cases.detail: Receive a ladder of nudges that lead you to the step rather than the final result.

use_cases.title: See the idea animated
use_cases.detail: Ask for the concept behind a mistake and watch a short generated animation of it.

pros: Works on your actual handwriting, not pasted text
Hint-first design deliberately avoids giving the answer
Runs against your own model subscription
cons: Built around xournal++ and a pen tablet
Early project with a single maintainer

name: Ambient Context
description: Ambient Context is a macOS menu bar app that writes down what you worked on during the day, in plain markdown, in a folder you own, so your AI assistant gets the context you actually saw. While it is open it reads the text of the focused window through the macOS accessibility tree and keeps a running record you can point Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or any MCP client at.
description_en: Ambient Context is a macOS menu bar app that writes down what you worked on during the day, in plain markdown, in a folder you own, so your AI assistant gets the context you actually saw. While it is open it reads the text of the focused window through the macOS accessibility tree and keeps a running record you can point Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or any MCP client at.

use_cases.title: Stop re-explaining your day
use_cases.detail: Hand your assistant the reading, writing and decisions it would otherwise never see.

use_cases.title: Own the log
use_cases.detail: Keep the record as plain markdown files in a folder on your own disk.

use_cases.title: Point any MCP client at it
use_cases.detail: Give Claude Code, Cursor or Codex access to the context folder directly.

pros: Plain markdown output you control
Free and open source, shipped as a signed and notarised DMG
Works with any MCP client
cons: macOS only, version 14 or later on Apple Silicon
Relies on the macOS accessibility tree to read window text

name: Lights-on Software Factory
description: A boilerplate repository for running a lights-on software factory with Claude Code. It packages the setup used on a real product: a container sandbox that shares only the workspace directory with the host, a deterministic bash command regulator that reduces approval friction, and an orchestrator the author reports cut token spend sharply compared with running Claude workflows directly.
description_en: A boilerplate repository for running a lights-on software factory with Claude Code. It packages the setup used on a real product: a container sandbox that shares only the workspace directory with the host, a deterministic bash command regulator that reduces approval friction, and an orchestrator the author reports cut token spend sharply compared with running Claude workflows directly.

use_cases.title: Start a sandboxed project
use_cases.detail: Run Claude Code in a container that shares only your workspace directory with the host machine.

use_cases.title: Cut the approval clicks
use_cases.detail: Use a deterministic command regulator so routine shell commands stop asking for permission.

use_cases.title: Study a worked factory
use_cases.detail: Read a complete, opinionated setup rather than assembling one from blog posts.

pros: Concrete repository you can clone and run today
Isolates the agent from the rest of your machine
Doubles as a teaching example of software factory concepts
cons: Opinionated: expects you to accept its structure
Oriented to Claude Code rather than other agent CLIs

name: Chess Postmortem Skills
description: Claude Code skills that turn one of your chess games into a post-mortem you can actually read: plain-language explanations of your mistakes checked against Stockfish, an annotated PGN, an HTML viewer and a narrated video of the whole game.
description_en: Claude Code skills that turn one of your chess games into a post-mortem you can actually read: plain-language explanations of your mistakes checked against Stockfish, an annotated PGN, an HTML viewer and a narrated video of the whole game.

use_cases.title: Explain the blunder in words
use_cases.detail: Turn a PGN into annotated commentary about what actually went wrong.

use_cases.title: Check it against an engine
use_cases.detail: Cross-check the plain-language advice with a Stockfish analysis.

use_cases.title: Review on video
use_cases.detail: Render a narrated video of the game to watch instead of reading a move list.

pros: Combines engine analysis with readable explanations
Ships an HTML viewer and a narrated video, not just text
Installs as skills inside Claude Code
cons: Narrow: one game at a time, chess only
Video rendering needs extra tooling on your machine

name: SIwithin
description: SIwithin runs an agent CLI unattended on a brief, inside a fence around the folders you give it and under a dollar budget, leaving one record per run. Your home folder is refused for both reading and writing, the run cannot spend more than the dollars it was given, and every run writes a line in a ledger saying what it did.
description_en: SIwithin runs an agent CLI unattended on a brief, inside a fence around the folders you give it and under a dollar budget, leaving one record per run. Your home folder is refused for both reading and writing, the run cannot spend more than the dollars it was given, and every run writes a line in a ledger saying what it did.

use_cases.title: Let it run overnight
use_cases.detail: Hand an agent a brief and walk away without supervising every command.

use_cases.title: Cap the spend
use_cases.detail: Set a budget per run and a cap across all runs, with a timer on each one.

use_cases.title: Keep a ledger
use_cases.detail: Get one line per run recording what the agent touched and what it cost.

pros: Enforces folder boundaries with a tool rather than trust
Per-run and global budget ceilings
Metered loopback proxy so the run never holds your API key
cons: New project with a very small user base
Some agent CLIs cannot be interrupted mid-run and are refused by default

name: Aura AI Agent
description: Aura is a self-hosted, multi-user AI agent written in Go. One binary hosts the runtime, tools, CLI, Telegram gateway and an embedded web cockpit, and each person signs in to their own identity with their own memory database and workspace. It ships with temporal graph memory, scheduled jobs, MCP tools and Telegram and WhatsApp channels as a Docker Compose appliance under the MIT licence.
description_en: Aura is a self-hosted, multi-user AI agent written in Go. One binary hosts the runtime, tools, CLI, Telegram gateway and an embedded web cockpit, and each person signs in to their own identity with their own memory database and workspace. It ships with temporal graph memory, scheduled jobs, MCP tools and Telegram and WhatsApp channels as a Docker Compose appliance under the MIT licence.

use_cases.title: One appliance for a team
use_cases.detail: Run a single agent host where every person gets their own identity, memory and workspace.

use_cases.title: Give agents a schedule
use_cases.detail: Set up scheduled jobs and document retrieval alongside interactive tool use.

use_cases.title: Reach it from chat
use_cases.detail: Talk to the same agent over Telegram or WhatsApp as well as the web cockpit.

pros: Provider-neutral and self-hosted on infrastructure you control
Per-person memory separation in one deployment
Ships as a Docker Compose appliance under MIT
cons: You operate the service and pay for your own models
Early-stage: expect to read the source to configure it

name: Yana
description: Yana is a local-first, cross-platform control plane that sits between any AI model and real power over your machine. It runs, connects, orchestrates and governs agents across cloud and local model providers, with deterministic control over what an agent can access, change and execute, plus pre, post and stop hooks around every tool call.
description_en: Yana is a local-first, cross-platform control plane that sits between any AI model and real power over your machine. It runs, connects, orchestrates and governs agents across cloud and local model providers, with deterministic control over what an agent can access, change and execute, plus pre, post and stop hooks around every tool call.

use_cases.title: Give tools without giving the keys
use_cases.detail: Hand an agent real capabilities with explicit, deterministic limits on each one.

use_cases.title: One runtime, many providers
use_cases.detail: Route the same governance layer across cloud models and local ones.

use_cases.title: Gate every call
use_cases.detail: Inspect and approve tool calls before they run, and react afterwards.

pros: Clear separation between what a model proposes and what it may do
Works across several agent hosts and model providers
Hooks before, after and on stop give real oversight
cons: Young project; the surface is large and still moving
Requires comfort with a CLI control plane

name: PageIndex
description: PageIndex is a document index for vectorless, reasoning-based retrieval. Instead of chunking text into a vector database it builds a tree index and lets a model reason over it, so retrieval is context-aware and reads the way a person skims a document. It ships a Python SDK with local and cloud modes and a file-level layer for reasoning across a whole corpus.
description_en: PageIndex is a document index for vectorless, reasoning-based retrieval. Instead of chunking text into a vector database it builds a tree index and lets a model reason over it, so retrieval is context-aware and reads the way a person skims a document. It ships a Python SDK with local and cloud modes and a file-level layer for reasoning across a whole corpus.

use_cases.title: Skip the vector database
use_cases.detail: Answer questions over long PDFs by reasoning over a tree index instead of embedding chunks.

use_cases.title: Run it on your own key
use_cases.detail: Index and retrieve locally on your machine with your own LLM API key.

use_cases.title: Search a whole corpus
use_cases.detail: Use the file-level layer to reason across many documents rather than one file at a time.

pros: No chunking and no vector store to tune
Local mode keeps documents and keys on your machine
Retrieval behaves like human skimming, which is easier to debug
cons: Reasoning-based retrieval costs more tokens per query than a vector lookup
Best results depend on the model doing the reasoning

name: OpenFlow
description: OpenFlow is a visual builder for multi-agent AI workflows. You drag role cards onto a canvas, wire a pipeline such as planner, architect and coder, save it, and run it with real parallel agents. It is built on and shipped as a fork of opencode, whose headless server drives execution.
description_en: OpenFlow is a visual builder for multi-agent AI workflows. You drag role cards onto a canvas, wire a pipeline such as planner, architect and coder, save it, and run it with real parallel agents. It is built on and shipped as a fork of opencode, whose headless server drives execution.

use_cases.title: Draw the pipeline
use_cases.detail: Lay out role cards and wire them together instead of editing configuration files by hand.

use_cases.title: Run roles in parallel
use_cases.detail: Execute a planner, an architect and a coder at the same time rather than in sequence.

use_cases.title: Reuse what worked
use_cases.detail: Save a pipeline and run it again on the next project.

pros: Canvas view makes multi-agent handoffs readable
Built on an existing headless agent engine rather than a toy runtime
Pipelines are saved and reusable
cons: Fork-based approach means upgrades can lag upstream
New project, so the edges are still rough

name: DocuMemory
description: DocuMemory is a memory engine that passively distils raw AI chat sessions into permanent architecture decisions and reusable, prompt-injectable context blocks. It captures sessions from Claude Code, ChatGPT, Cursor and Windsurf, strips noise through subtractive distillation, then recalls and injects what matters into the next session over MCP.
description_en: DocuMemory is a memory engine that passively distils raw AI chat sessions into permanent architecture decisions and reusable, prompt-injectable context blocks. It captures sessions from Claude Code, ChatGPT, Cursor and Windsurf, strips noise through subtractive distillation, then recalls and injects what matters into the next session over MCP.

use_cases.title: Keep the decisions, drop the chat
use_cases.detail: Turn long sessions into architecture decision records you can read later.

use_cases.title: Start every session informed
use_cases.detail: Inject distilled context blocks into the next session automatically.

use_cases.title: Work across clients
use_cases.detail: Capture from Claude Code, ChatGPT, Cursor, Windsurf or any MCP client.

pros: Aimed at decisions rather than raw transcript storage
MCP-native, so it drops into the clients you already use
Promises hybrid search with sub-50ms recall
cons: Hosted service with a sign-up, not something you self-host
Value depends on how much of your work happens in chat sessions
