use_cases.detail: The server holds secrets and controls, observability and the file server, and the network joins it to every worker.

pros: Self-hosted on hardware you already have, including an old PC
Secrets, controls and observability sit in one server
Install scripts for Linux, macOS and Windows
cons: Needs a machine left running to be useful
The architecture diagrams carry most of the explanation, with written detail in separate docs

name: MindThread MCP
description: MindThread MCP is a Threads scheduler built for AI agents. Through Meta's official Threads API it lets Claude, Cursor or any MCP client write, schedule and publish posts, review drafted replies and read insights, with 40+ tools and per-permission controls.
description_en: MindThread MCP is a Threads scheduler built for AI agents. Through Meta's official Threads API it lets Claude, Cursor or any MCP client write, schedule and publish posts, review drafted replies and read insights, with 40+ tools and per-permission controls.
best_for: Scheduling Threads posts from an AI agent
Keeping an agent's posting inside brand rules
Reviewing drafted replies before they go out

use_cases.title: Write and schedule
use_cases.detail: Generate one to five drafts in the account's voice, or threads of two to ten parts, then publish text, a single image, a carousel or video, now or at an exact time.

use_cases.title: Enforce content rules
use_cases.detail: Length limits, banned phrases, no hashtags and only numbers from your fact list are enforced by the server rather than suggested in a prompt.

use_cases.title: Approve before posting
use_cases.detail: Every key has per-permission allow, ask or deny; with ask, the post waits until you confirm it.

pros: Content rules are enforced server-side instead of being asked for in a prompt
Per-permission allow, ask or deny on every key
Cloud patrol searches Threads for your keywords and drafts replies for you to approve or reject
cons: Bound to Threads and to Meta's official API
A free sandbox key is offered, which suggests it is early

name: Kashkeshet
description: Kashkeshet is an MCP server written in Rust that lets your AI agents set up chat channels and talk to each other. It is deliberately non-opinionated: it hands agents a basic set of primitives and leaves how they use them to you and to them.
description_en: Kashkeshet is an MCP server written in Rust that lets your AI agents set up chat channels and talk to each other. It is deliberately non-opinionated: it hands agents a basic set of primitives and leaves how they use them to you and to them.
best_for: Letting several agents talk to each other
Watching agent-to-agent conversation from a web page
Running agent chat on localhost or a tailnet

use_cases.title: Install and serve
use_cases.detail: Install with the release script on macOS or Linux, then run kkt service install to start it at each login, or kkt serve in a terminal.

use_cases.title: Connect your clients
use_cases.detail: The server listens on localhost at 127.0.0.1:7420, and every client and the web page share an access key that kkt creates for you.

use_cases.title: Watch the conversation
use_cases.detail: A web page lets you monitor the channels your agents set up and the messages going between them.

pros: Gives agents primitives rather than a prescribed workflow
A web page for monitoring what the agents are actually saying
Installs as a background service and starts again at login
cons: Security is minimal by design: it prevents accidental connections and nothing more
Intended for localhost or a network you control, such as a tailnet

name: Free ASR
description: Free ASR is a zero-dependency, pure-Swift real-time streaming speech-to-text client and complete protocol specification, reverse-engineered from Doubao Input Method for macOS. It documents what the gateway actually validates and what it does not.
description_en: Free ASR is a zero-dependency, pure-Swift real-time streaming speech-to-text client and complete protocol specification, reverse-engineered from Doubao Input Method for macOS. It documents what the gateway actually validates and what it does not.
best_for: Streaming speech-to-text on macOS without an account
Understanding how a commercial ASR WebSocket gateway authenticates
Building a Swift ASR client with no dependencies

use_cases.title: Stream audio
use_cases.detail: A pure-Swift client for the streaming ASR WebSocket gateway, which works without signing into an account.

use_cases.title: Read the protocol
use_cases.detail: The repository documents how authentication and streaming work, including which fields the server checks and which it ignores.

use_cases.title: Generate a device id
use_cases.detail: Any randomly generated 16-digit numeric string is accepted; the server uses device_id only for rate-limiting buckets and log tracing.

pros: Zero dependencies and pure Swift
Documents the protocol rather than only shipping a binary
No account login and no device registration required
cons: Reverse-engineered from a commercial app, so it can break without notice
Rate limiting still applies through the device_id bucket

name: Skill Spotter
description: Skill Spotter is a Claude Code plugin that notices tasks you keep repeating and offers to save them as a skill you can run with /name. It compares what Claude did, not just what you typed, so a rephrased request still counts.
description_en: Skill Spotter is a Claude Code plugin that notices tasks you keep repeating and offers to save them as a skill you can run with /name. It compares what Claude did, not just what you typed, so a rephrased request still counts.
best_for: Turning repeated Claude Code requests into reusable skills

use_cases.title: Spot the repeat
use_cases.detail: After the third request of a kind, a band offers to create a named skill; Claude drafts it, and next time /name does the task.

use_cases.title: Match the task, not the words
use_cases.detail: It compares the commands, files and tools Claude used as well as your prompt, and it also spots multi-prompt workflows.

use_cases.title: Retire repeated rules
use_cases.detail: When you add the same instruction to many different requests, it offers to put it in CLAUDE.md instead.

pros: Everything stays on your computer, with no upload, telemetry or account
Uses no tokens per turn; suggestions are shown to you, not to Claude
Never creates a skill on its own; you decide with /skill-spotter:draft
cons: Claude Code only, and demonstrated in a session of version 2.1.308
It only suggests; running the draft command is still up to you

name: App Factory
description: App Factory is a Claude Code plugin marketplace of 42 skills in eight opt-in tracks that build, describe, ship and announce apps to the App Store, Google Play, and directly on Mac and Windows. You enable only the tracks a repo needs.
description_en: App Factory is a Claude Code plugin marketplace of 42 skills in eight opt-in tracks that build, describe, ship and announce apps to the App Store, Google Play, and directly on Mac and Windows. You enable only the tracks a repo needs.
best_for: Shipping an app to the App Store or Google Play with an agent
Loading only the skills a given repository needs
Automating store metadata and release announcements

use_cases.title: Add the marketplace
use_cases.detail: Run claude plugin marketplace add yybd/app-factory, then enable.py picks the tracks for your repo and prints the install lines.

use_cases.title: Check a name
use_cases.detail: The skills ship ordinary command-line scripts, including check_name.py, which audits a name against the live App Store.

use_cases.title: Catch a dropped claim
use_cases.detail: measure_copy.py catches a translation that dropped a claim from the original copy.

pros: Opt-in tracks mean a session only carries the skills that repo needs
The scripts are ordinary command-line tools, not agent-only magic
QUICKSTART walks the whole thing in about fifteen minutes, for one app
cons: Built for Claude Code and tested only there; most skills find scripts through CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT
42 skills across eight tracks is a lot to learn before it pays off

name: SuperCMO Skills
description: SuperCMO Skills are open source skills that let any AI agent generate end-to-end marketing campaigns. You provide a product photo and a brief; the agent extracts product details, selects image and video models, casts AI actors and edits the result.
description_en: SuperCMO Skills are open source skills that let any AI agent generate end-to-end marketing campaigns. You provide a product photo and a brief; the agent extracts product details, selects image and video models, casts AI actors and edits the result.
best_for: Generating UGC and ad videos from one product photo
Keeping actors and products consistent across a campaign
Running marketing generation in Claude Code, Cursor or Codex

use_cases.title: Install into your agent
use_cases.detail: One npx command installs the skills into Claude Code, Cursor and Codex; for Cursor you add --cursor --project-dir . so they land in the project too.

use_cases.title: Give it a photo and a brief
use_cases.detail: The agent extracts the product details, picks the models, casts AI actors and edits the generated content into finished assets.

use_cases.title: Make longer pieces
use_cases.detail: It can produce videos of any length while maintaining actor and product consistency.

pros: One command installs into several different agents
Actor and product consistency is an explicit goal rather than a side effect
Apache-2.0 licensed and open source, as an alternative to closed marketing agents
cons: Installation requires uv
Output quality depends on the external image and video models it routes to

name: Bitty
description: Bitty fills the gaps while your AI works, with brain games sized to the wait. You hit a shortcut or tell it roughly how long the agent will take, and a math, memory, pattern, logic, estimate or code challenge is already there.
description_en: Bitty fills the gaps while your AI works, with brain games sized to the wait. You hit a shortcut or tell it roughly how long the agent will take, and a math, memory, pattern, logic, estimate or code challenge is already there.
best_for: Filling short waits while an agent runs
Avoiding the scroll that turns thirty seconds into eight minutes
Getting back to work the moment the agent finishes

use_cases.title: Start a challenge
use_cases.detail: Hit the shortcut when the agent starts working, or tell Bitty roughly how long it will take.

use_cases.title: Play to the clock
use_cases.detail: Challenges are sized to the wait, from a five second blitz upward, so you choose how long the AI is taking rather than which game.

use_cases.title: Bow out instantly
use_cases.detail: Press Esc and the challenge leaves mid-question; the site is explicit that work always wins.

pros: Free, with direct downloads for macOS, Windows and Linux and no app store
Works offline
Esc exits immediately, so it never competes with the actual work
cons: Only useful if your agent really does leave you waiting
The games are deliberately tiny, so it is not a general training app

name: Roadster AI
description: Roadster AI turns a photo of your car into a stunt video. You choose one of six stunts, upload a photo with the whole vehicle in frame and all wheels visible, and get a short clip of lift-off, a roll over a line of cars and a landing.
description_en: Roadster AI turns a photo of your car into a stunt video. You choose one of six stunts, upload a photo with the whole vehicle in frame and all wheels visible, and get a short clip of lift-off, a roll over a line of cars and a landing.
best_for: Turning a car photo into a stunt clip
Making product ads that borrow the same stunt format

use_cases.title: Pick a stunt
use_cases.detail: Six stunts are available to preview: ramp flip, ramp kickflip, side kickflip, trackside kickflip, thruster close-up and overhead ramp.

use_cases.title: Upload your car or product
use_cases.detail: Cars, SUVs, trucks and bikes, or products for ads; JPG, PNG or WebP up to 20 MB, with the whole vehicle in frame and all wheels visible.

use_cases.title: Choose a shape
use_cases.detail: Output comes in 16:9, 9:16 and 1:1, with sound effects.

pros: One narrow, well-defined output instead of a generic text-to-video prompt box
Products can stand in for cars, which makes it usable for ads
Three aspect ratios for different social surfaces
cons: One trick, tied to a specific stunt format
The upload rules are strict: whole vehicle in frame, all wheels visible, side or three-quarter view

name: JSONEx Lab
description: JSONEx Lab classifies products into HS (Harmonized System) customs codes with AI. Type a product description and get a six to ten digit code with a confidence score, through the web form, a REST API, an MCP server or a Google Sheets add-on.
description_en: JSONEx Lab classifies products into HS (Harmonized System) customs codes with AI. Type a product description and get a six to ten digit code with a confidence score, through the web form, a REST API, an MCP server or a Google Sheets add-on.
best_for: Classifying products for import and export
Adding HS code lookup to an AI agent over MCP

use_cases.title: Classify one product
use_cases.detail: Type a product on the home page with no signup and get a code with a confidence score; the example returns 8471.30 at 90% for an iPhone 15 Pro.

use_cases.title: Call it from an agent
use_cases.detail: There is a REST API, a Model Context Protocol server for AI agents, and a Google Sheets add-on.

use_cases.title: Do a whole catalogue
use_cases.detail: Batch up to 100 items in a single request.

pros: Free tier of 50 classifications a day with no credit card and no signup
Four surfaces: web form, REST API, MCP server and Google Sheets
x402 payments let an agent pay per call in USDC on Base without an API key
cons: The free tier is capped at 50 classifications a day
Confidence is a model estimate, so customs-critical work still needs checking

name: Heldkeys
description: Heldkeys answers one question: if a prompt injection hijacked the AI agent running here, which credentials could it use? It lists them for your terminal, the agent's sandbox or the CI job, without printing a single secret.
description_en: Heldkeys answers one question: if a prompt injection hijacked the AI agent running here, which credentials could it use? It lists them for your terminal, the agent's sandbox or the CI job, without printing a single secret.
best_for: Seeing which credentials an agent can reach
Checking a CI job for risky agent steps

use_cases.title: List what is reachable
use_cases.detail: Run it in the terminal, inside the agent's sandbox, or in CI to see which credentials are in reach there.

use_cases.title: Check GitHub workflows
use_cases.detail: It flags risky AI agent steps in GitHub workflows.

use_cases.title: Keep secrets out of output
use_cases.detail: The README is explicit that it never prints secrets, and the project carries a badge saying so.

pros: Answers one concrete threat-model question rather than scanning broadly
Works in the terminal, the sandbox and CI
Never prints a secret
cons: It lists what is reachable; deciding what to remove is still yours
Scoped to the machine it runs on rather than a fleet

name: Termexo
description: Termexo is a Windows workbench where one AI operates your other coding agents. It works with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Antigravity and Grok Build: you see which agent needs you, resume sessions, and reconnect from your phone.
description_en: Termexo is a Windows workbench where one AI operates your other coding agents. It works with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Antigravity and Grok Build: you see which agent needs you, resume sessions, and reconnect from your phone.
best_for: Running several coding agents on Windows
Seeing which agent is waiting for you
Resuming an agent session from your phone

use_cases.title: Install on Windows
use_cases.detail: A Tauri 2 desktop app at version 0.11.0, also published to npm, with downloads on the releases page.

use_cases.title: Watch your agents
use_cases.detail: See which agent needs you instead of checking each one yourself.

use_cases.title: Resume from elsewhere
use_cases.detail: Resume sessions and reconnect from your phone.

pros: Covers several agent harnesses at once rather than one
Phone reconnects mean you are not tied to the Windows machine
Open source, and also installable from npm
cons: Windows only
It sits above your agents, so it is another thing to keep updated

name: Ecsodus
description: Ecsodus migrates AWS Copilot CLI apps to Terraform-managed ECS in place, with no downtime and no data loss. It inventories, reports, generates, retain-patches, imports and tears down, as a read-only, gated runbook.
description_en: Ecsodus migrates AWS Copilot CLI apps to Terraform-managed ECS in place, with no downtime and no data loss. It inventories, reports, generates, retain-patches, imports and tears down, as a read-only, gated runbook.
best_for: Leaving AWS Copilot CLI after support ended
Moving ECS apps to Terraform without an outage
Importing existing infrastructure instead of rebuilding it

use_cases.title: Inventory and report
use_cases.detail: Read-only steps come first, so you see what would change before anything does.

use_cases.title: Generate and import
use_cases.detail: Terraform is generated, then existing resources are imported, with retain patches applied so teardown cannot delete them.

use_cases.title: Tear down safely
use_cases.detail: The Copilot stack is removed only after the import has been verified.

pros: Migration in place with no downtime and no data loss as the stated goal
Read-only first, and the runbook is gated
A documented end-to-end run on AWS reports 44 of 44 imports and zero data loss
cons: Narrow in scope: AWS Copilot CLI to Terraform on ECS only
Needs Terraform 1.10 or newer and Python

name: Squeeze
description: Squeeze reads a tool's output on stdin and prints only what an agent acts on: every change, failure and decision, plus a note naming what it cut. It detects the format, so a terraform plan of 6,294 bytes comes back as 485.
description_en: Squeeze reads a tool's output on stdin and prints only what an agent acts on: every change, failure and decision, plus a note naming what it cut. It detects the format, so a terraform plan of 6,294 bytes comes back as 485.
best_for: Cutting the tokens an agent spends reading tool output
Piping test and plan output into an agent
Keeping context for decisions instead of noise

use_cases.title: Pipe it
use_cases.detail: squeeze detects the format: run go test -json ./... 2>&1 | squeeze, or terraform show -json plan.out | squeeze.

use_cases.title: Tell your agent
use_cases.detail: Add a line to AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md telling the agent to pipe long tool output through squeeze, in the tool's JSON mode when it has one.

use_cases.title: Recover the detail
use_cases.detail: Rerun with the flag squeeze names, such as --max-attrs 0, only when the output lacks what you need.

pros: Detects the format, so you just pipe
Names what it cut, so the agent knows something was removed
Installs with go install and needs no running service
cons: No release yet; the output can change until 1.0
Lossy by design, so the agent may need a rerun with a flag

name: Scaled Thought
description: Scaled Thought is an OpenAI-compatible API for open-weight models. Paste one line and your coding agent sets up models, keys and budgets itself, or point your existing OpenAI SDK at the base URL and pay per token from prepaid credits.
description_en: Scaled Thought is an OpenAI-compatible API for open-weight models. Paste one line and your coding agent sets up models, keys and budgets itself, or point your existing OpenAI SDK at the base URL and pay per token from prepaid credits.
best_for: Giving a coding agent its own model budget
Calling open-weight models through the OpenAI SDK
Prepaid per-token spend instead of a subscription

use_cases.title: Let the agent sign up
use_cases.detail: Paste one line into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any agent that can run commands, or run npx -y scaledthought@0.5 init yourself.

use_cases.title: Keep your SDK code
use_cases.detail: Change the base URL and keep using the OpenAI SDK, with models such as MiMo-V2.6-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.

use_cases.title: Pay per token
use_cases.detail: Usage is billed from prepaid credits rather than a monthly subscription.

pros: OpenAI-compatible, so existing code keeps working
An agent can provision its own key and budget
Prepaid credits keep the spend bounded
cons: Prepaid credits only, with no subscription option described
The free usage offer is limited to new accounts in the US region and expires after 30 days

name: Nyrion
description: Nyrion is practice for the new AI-assisted coding interview format. Each problem is a small multi-stage repository, an AI assistant sits in the editor with you, and passing tests unlocks stages that escalate the requirements.
description_en: Nyrion is practice for the new AI-assisted coding interview format. Each problem is a small multi-stage repository, an AI assistant sits in the editor with you, and passing tests unlocks stages that escalate the requirements.
best_for: Reading unfamiliar code under time pressure
Practising directing an agent rather than typing

use_cases.title: Open a real codebase
use_cases.detail: Problems are small multi-stage repositories rather than isolated snippets.

use_cases.title: Direct the agent
use_cases.detail: The assistant sits in the editor with you; the posture is full execution and zero novel ideas, so you stay the architect.

use_cases.title: Pass to escalate
use_cases.detail: Tests gate progression, so passing them unlocks stricter requirements.

pros: Matches the format that Meta, Shopify, Canva, LinkedIn and Rippling are described as using
Stage-gated progression mirrors how interviewers raise the bar in the room
Tests reading unfamiliar code and directing an assistant, not puzzle recall
cons: No pricing shown on the landing page
Only worth the time if you are actually interviewing in this format

name: XCrashlytics
description: XCrashlytics is a macOS CLI for Firebase Crashlytics and local Xcode Organizer reports. It gives you and your coding agent access to crash messages, app stacks and impact reports without copying data out of the console by hand.
description_en: XCrashlytics is a macOS CLI for Firebase Crashlytics and local Xcode Organizer reports. It gives you and your coding agent access to crash messages, app stacks and impact reports without copying data out of the console by hand.
best_for: Investigating production crashes from the terminal
Giving a coding agent real crash context

use_cases.title: Start with a question
use_cases.detail: Begin from something like what is crashing checkout since the last release, rather than from a dashboard.

use_cases.title: Pull the evidence
use_cases.detail: It reads crash messages, app stacks and impact reports from Firebase Crashlytics, and on iOS also reads reports Xcode has already downloaded.

use_cases.title: Hand it to the agent
use_cases.detail: The argument is that your agent cannot investigate evidence it has never seen.

pros: Works with iOS, Android, macOS and other Crashlytics apps
Also reads Xcode Organizer reports already sitting on disk
Swift 6.0, MIT licensed, macOS 15 or newer
cons: macOS only
Needs Crashlytics or Xcode data to exist before it is useful

name: Truth Firewall
description: Truth Firewall independently verifies your acceptance conditions before accepting DONE from a coding agent, and returns VERIFIED_DONE, REJECT_DONE or HUMAN_REQUIRED. The agent does the work; Truth Firewall decides whether DONE was earned.
description_en: Truth Firewall independently verifies your acceptance conditions before accepting DONE from a coding agent, and returns VERIFIED_DONE, REJECT_DONE or HUMAN_REQUIRED. The agent does the work; Truth Firewall decides whether DONE was earned.
best_for: Verifying an agent really finished the task
Catching skipped requirements and broken edge cases
Stopping the habit of re-checking everything yourself

use_cases.title: Install it
use_cases.detail: Install with pipx on Python 3.11 or newer, then run truth-firewall --version and truth-firewall demo.

use_cases.title: Give Codex the task
use_cases.detail: Codex works, says DONE, and Truth Firewall verifies the required work before anything is accepted.

use_cases.title: Read the verdict
use_cases.detail: The result is one of VERIFIED_DONE, REJECT_DONE or HUMAN_REQUIRED; on a rejection, Codex keeps working.

pros: Three explicit outcomes instead of a vague pass
Verifies acceptance conditions independently of what the agent reported
A demo runs offline without a Codex account
cons: Authenticated Codex execution in 0.1.0 is a Windows-only pilot
You still have to write the acceptance conditions

name: ESP32 Pie ASR
description: ESP32 Pie ASR runs live English speech recognition on an ESP32-P4: a 65.7M-parameter streaming Zipformer2 transducer whose weights were brought from 71 MB to 26.65 MB in 2 and 4 bits, running faster than real time on the chip alone.
description_en: ESP32 Pie ASR runs live English speech recognition on an ESP32-P4: a 65.7M-parameter streaming Zipformer2 transducer whose weights were brought from 71 MB to 26.65 MB in 2 and 4 bits, running faster than real time on the chip alone.
best_for: On-device speech recognition on a microcontroller
Voice control with no cloud and no neural accelerator
Streaming ASR on RISC-V cores with PIE SIMD

use_cases.title: Flash from the browser
use_cases.detail: The project page flashes the firmware straight from your browser, and releases are published on GitHub.

use_cases.title: Speak to the board
use_cases.detail: The board's microphone in, the words on its screen as you speak, with no cloud and no neural accelerator.

use_cases.title: Try the demos
use_cases.detail: Six voice-control demos ship with the firmware.

pros: Open vocabulary streaming ASR that runs faster than real time on a microcontroller
Weights are published on Hugging Face, built from Banafo's Kroko model
Firmware builds are automated, and you can flash from a browser
cons: English only, and tied to the ESP32-P4
Quantising to 2 and 4 bits trades accuracy for fitting on the chip
